readerTitle: The yes is not the end of the sale
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 단체 예약, 소프트웨어 연간 계약) + 실제 연구 (Festinger 1957 인지 부조화, Ehrlich 외 1957 신차 구매자 광고 열람 연구)
insight: 판매 전에 해결한 반론은 사라지지 않고 계약 직후 조용히 되돌아온다. 판매는 돈을 받을 때가 아니라 고객이 잘 골랐다고 확신할 때 끝난다.
misconception: 고객이 '예'라고 하고 돈을 내면 반론 처리는 끝났고, 다음 연락은 납품이나 갱신 때 하면 된다.

sources.text: Festinger, L. (1957). A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance. Stanford University Press.
Ehrlich, D., Guttman, I., Schönbach, P., & Mills, J. (1957). Postdecision exposure to relevant information. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 54(1), 98–102.
레스토랑과 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Ehrlich 외(1957) 연구: 최근 신차 구매자가 다른 후보 차량보다 자신이 산 차의 광고를 더 많이 읽었다는 결과. 원문에서 방향성을 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 수치 없이 결과 방향만 적었습니다.
Festinger의 인지 부조화 이론 출간 연도(1957)와 정의 문구가 원저와 맞는지 확인하세요.
레스토랑(40명 단체 예약, 6주 후 행사)과 진료소(20명, 연간 계약) 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 수치는 상황 설명용입니다.

cards.title: The yes is not the end of the sale
body: A restaurant books a private dinner for 40 guests. A software company signs a clinic to a yearly plan. Both customers say yes on Monday.
By Friday, both are quietly wondering if they made a mistake. Only one business notices in time.

image.label: Two customers after signing, one with a worried thought bubble
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 레스토랑 예약 확인서를 든 고객, 오른쪽은 노트북 앞의 진료소 관리자. 두 사람 모두 계약 직후인데 머리 위에 작은 물음표 말풍선. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The deposit just cleared.
body: You run a restaurant. A client just paid a deposit for a private dinner for 40 guests, six weeks away. During the sale she worried about two things: the price, and whether vegetarian guests would eat well.
What do you do in the next two days?

options.text: Send the receipt and get in touch closer to the date
options.feedback: It saves time now, but it leaves her alone with both worries for six weeks. That's a long time for doubt to grow.

options.text: Send a warm thank-you and plan a check-in call in a month
options.feedback: Friendly, and better than silence. But a thank-you doesn't answer the vegetarian worry, and a month is late.

options.text: Next day, send a note with what's included, a sample vegetarian menu and a tasting date
options.feedback: It costs a little effort, but it answers her exact worry with something she can see and share. The next cards show why that matters.

cards.title: Same booking, two different weeks.
body: Picture two restaurants with the same booking. The first sends a receipt and goes quiet. The client sees a cheaper venue online, remembers her vegetarian worry, and emails to ask about cancelling.
The second sends a short note the next day: what's included, a sample vegetarian menu, a tasting date. The client forwards it to her boss. Now she has **proof she chose well**.

image.label: Two timelines after a booking: one quiet, one with a follow-up
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 두 줄. 윗줄은 '예약' 이후 빈 칸이 이어지다 '취소 문의'로 끝남(회색 톤). 아랫줄은 '예약' 다음 날 '메뉴와 시식 일정 안내', 이어서 '상사에게 전달'(밝은 톤). 로고 없음.

cards.title: Post-purchase doubt
body: **Post-purchase doubt**, often called buyer's remorse, is the worry that arrives right after a customer commits. The objections you answered during the sale don't disappear. They go quiet, then come back when the customer is alone with the decision.
So the sale isn't finished when the customer pays. It's finished when they feel sure they chose well.

cards.title: People look for reassurance after they decide.
body: In 1957, psychologist Leon Festinger described **cognitive dissonance**: the discomfort of holding a choice and a doubt at the same time. People work to make that discomfort go away.

The same year, a study of new car owners found they read more ads for the car they had just bought than for the cars they had passed over. Buyers go looking for proof. If you don't give it to them, they may find doubts instead.

cards.title: Three moves in the first days.
body: Good follow-up after the sale does three things:
list: **Confirm:** restate what they bought and why it fits them
**Close the loop:** answer the objection they raised, with something concrete
**Show an early win:** give them a first result they can see or share
cards.callout: Speed matters. Doubt grows in the quiet days right after the yes.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the quiet days are the first week after signing. Users who never reach a first real result are the ones most likely to churn at renewal.

cards.title: Reassurance is not pressure.
body: Follow-up should answer real doubts, not bury them. Flattery, extra promises or constant check-ins can make a buyer more nervous, not less.
And sometimes the doubt is right. If the product truly doesn't fit, helping the customer out early often costs less than a bitter refund later. It also protects your reputation.

cards.title: Now it's a software contract.
body: Your company sells scheduling software. A 20-person clinic just signed a yearly plan. During the sale, the office manager said her biggest fear was that setup would eat weeks of her staff's time.

options.text: Send logins and a help center link, then check in before renewal
options.feedback: Cheap for you, but it leaves her alone with the exact fear she raised. The doubt can grow quietly until renewal.

options.text: Book a 30-minute setup call where her team schedules one real day of appointments
options.feedback: It answers her setup fear with proof and gives her an early win to show her staff. It costs you a call and saves a much harder renewal.

options.text: Send a welcome email listing all your best features
options.feedback: Quick and friendly, but it answers a question she didn't ask. Her worry was time, not features.

cards.title: A sale ends when the customer feels sure.
body: The objections you answered before the yes come back after it. Meet them first, fast, and with proof.
**Try it today:** pick your last three new customers. Write down the worry each one raised before buying. Has anyone answered it since?
